name: The St Paul's Churchyard Planes

location.address: North Churchyard, St Paul's Cathedral, City of London EC4M 8AD

access: Free, open access, public churchyard garden on the north side of St Paul's Cathedral (no ticket needed for the garden, only for the cathedral interior)
transport: 2 min walk from St Paul's station (Central Line)
verify_notes: Three large London planes stand on the north side of St Paul's Cathedral churchyard, in a public garden distinct from the already-published Cheapside Plane (lon_003), which stands about 400m away at the Wood Street/Cheapside corner. Source 1 (a detailed local-history blog post) states directly: 'On the north side there are three large plane trees (a fourth had to be removed after a storm in 1987). They are ancient, perhaps over 250 years old, so somebody planted them in the middle of the 18th century... Like the cathedral, they have survived the Blitz.' Source 2, the official London Parks & Gardens Trust inventory record for the churchyard (site ID COL096), independently corroborates: 'In the north are some of the oldest plane trees in the City.' The precise '250+ years' figure and the 1987-storm/fourth-tree detail come from source 1 only; source 2 corroborates the general claim (oldest plane trees in the City) but not the exact number or age. Flagged for that reason, and because this is an ensemble of three unnamed trees rather than one named specimen (compact, one obvious place to stand: the paved path along the north side of the churchyard). No individual tree-level coordinates found in any source; the location given is the churchyard garden's approximate centre on its north side. Good material for the writer: same churchyard as the cathedral that replaced Old St Paul's after the Great Fire, planted mid-18th century when the current cathedral was still relatively new, survived both the Blitz and the Great Storm of 1987 (which took the fourth tree of the original group). Distance from the Cheapside Plane anchor (lon_003): approximately 0.39 km, well within a single walk.

name: The Amwell Street Fig

location.address: Amwell Street, outside the former Clerkenwell Parochial Schools building, EC1R

access: Free, open access, standing against a street frontage on public pavement
transport: 8 min walk from Angel station (Northern Line) or Farringdon station
verify_notes: A sprawling, multi-branched, prop-supported common fig, actually more than one stem/trunk from the same rootstock, growing against the former Clerkenwell Parochial Schools building on Amwell Street. Source 1 (Paul Wood, The Street Tree, a specialist London-tree newsletter) states it 'has probably been here since the schools opened' and was 'intentionally planted in front of the Clerkenwell Parochial Schools', 'possibly, in part, to help illustrate biblical stories' (article partly paywalled; this is the quoted portion available). One source (the Amwell Society's own history page) dates the Parochial School building to 1830, not 1827 as some secondary summaries claim; treat the exact founding year as 1827-1830 and the tree's age as approximate rather than precise. Source 2, monumentaltrees.com, corroborates the tree's existence, species, exact street and general location (used for verification only, per the hard rule, not as the source of any fact stated above). FLAGGED for two reasons: (1) the age claim rests on one substantive source rather than two independent ones, since monumentaltrees only verifies existence/location, not age; (2) distance from the Cheapside Plane anchor (lon_003) is approximately 2.0 km straight-line, likely 2.3-2.5 km on foot, at or just past the edge of 'roughly 2 km' from the rest of this City of London cluster. Recommend the main session judge whether this joins the St Paul's/Cheapside walk as a short detour or is held for a separate Clerkenwell cluster. Good material for the writer: an intentionally planted fig outside a Victorian charity school, a nice human-history angle distinct from the royal-park/churchyard stories that dominate London's list, and Islington still records it as a notable street tree today.

name: The Dorchester Plane

location.address: Forecourt of The Dorchester Hotel, 53 Park Lane, Mayfair, London W1K 1QA

access: Free, stands in The Dorchester Hotel's open forecourt directly on Park Lane, clearly visible and reachable from the public pavement without entering the hotel
transport: 8 min walk from Hyde Park Corner station (Piccadilly Line)
verify_notes: A large London plane with a prominent above-ground root system, standing in the landscaped forecourt at the south end of the Dorchester Hotel on Park Lane, Mayfair. Named one of the 'Great Trees of London' by the London Tree Forum and Countryside Commission in 1997 (Wikipedia's Great Trees of London list, sourced to Paul Wood's 'Great Trees of London Map', Blue Crow Media, 2020, gives coordinates 51.506828, -0.152099 and states it was 'planted in the early 1930s'). Two independent blog sources (Exploring London, Know Your London) corroborate the tree's existence, species and exact forecourt location but add no age detail beyond the 1997 designation. The 1930s planting date lines up with the hotel's own history: The Dorchester opened in 1931, so a tree planted for the new building's forecourt in the 'early 1930s' fits, though no source ties the two facts together explicitly. FLAGGED because the specific age comes from one dedicated source (the Great Trees map/book) rather than two independent ones; the hotel-opening coincidence is corroborating context, not a second citation. The tree reportedly featured in a BBC documentary, 'Meetings with Remarkable Trees' (2000), per secondary mentions; not independently confirmed in this pass and worth citing cautiously if at all. A 2020s hotel-renovation feature (Hotel Designs, 'The Dorchester's new look') describes the forecourt's 'landscaped, verdant garden area located underneath the renowned plane tree', which is decent circumstantial evidence the tree was still standing during the hotel's most recent facade refit. Good material for the writer: a soot-tolerant hybrid plane standing sentinel over one of London's most photographed hotel entrances since the Art Deco era, its swollen root plate now a minor local landmark in its own right.

name: The Marylebone Elm

location.address: Pavement outside the Memorial Garden of Rest, 65 Marylebone High Street, Westminster, London W1U

access: Free, stands on the open public pavement directly outside the small Garden of Rest, no restriction
transport: 6 min walk from Baker Street station (Bakerloo, Circle, District, Hammersmith & City, Jubilee, Metropolitan Lines)
verify_notes: A mature elm literally marooned on the pavement of Marylebone High Street, beside the tiny Memorial Garden of Rest that occupies the site of the old St Marylebone parish church (demolished after WWII bomb damage; the garden was created in 1951). Three independent sources agree it is a Huntingdon Elm (Ulmus x hollandica 'Vegeta', a Wych x Field elm hybrid), estimated at approximately 150 years old as of the 2010s (Wikipedia's Great Trees of London list, citing Paul Wood's 2020 map/book, gives coordinates 51.521886, -0.151724 and 'over 100 feet high'; londontreesblog.wordpress.com, 2014, gives the same ~150-year estimate and the Huntingdon Elm ID; bugwomanlondon.com, March 2017, independently repeats ~150 years and includes photos of the tree in bud, confirming it alive and healthy at that date). Aged forward from a consistent ~150-year estimate given across 2010s sources, the tree is roughly 160-165 years old by 2026; treat the age as an estimate rather than a precise figure. ALIVE NOW: a 27 April 2026 blog post (writerinthegarden.com) independently describes the same tree still standing prominently on the High Street pavement, 'as if it has escaped the park and is venturing out to cross the road', which is strong, very recent alive-evidence, though that one post loosely calls it 'a Wych elm' rather than the more specific Huntingdon Elm cultivar the specialist tree sources use; note this minor species-label discrepancy for the writer rather than silently picking a name. History: the last Huntingdon elm in Westminster to have escaped Dutch elm disease (which killed over 25 million UK elms from the 1960s on, ~75% of the national population), and it also survived the Blitz that demolished the parish church beside it, leaving the tree as effectively the church's last physical trace. A genuinely good story: a species-extinction survivor and a Blitz survivor in one trunk, on a pavement most Londoners walk straight past.

name: The Embankment Plane

location.address: North side of Horse Guards Avenue at the junction with Victoria Embankment, Westminster, London SW1A

access: Free, stands on the public pavement/verge at the Horse Guards Avenue and Victoria Embankment junction, fully open access, no restriction
transport: 7 min walk from Westminster station (Circle, District, Jubilee Lines)
verify_notes: One of the 'Great Trees of London', standing on the north side of Horse Guards Avenue at its junction with Victoria Embankment. Wikipedia's Great Trees of London list (sourced to Paul Wood's 'Great Trees of London Map', Blue Crow Media, 2020) gives coordinates 51.504796, -0.123285, identifies the species as Oriental Plane (Platanus orientalis, not the usual London Plane hybrid) and states it was 'planted in 1870'. That specific date and species claim rest on one dedicated source; general histories of the Victoria Embankment (Southbank Centre's 'City and tree: the story of London planes'; Trees for Cities' 'The mysterious story of the London plane tree') independently corroborate that planes were planted along the newly built Victoria Embankment starting around 1870, the first systematically tree-planted scheme of its kind in the city, but neither names this individual tree. FLAGGED because the individual-tree date and species rest on the one specialist source, corroborated only by general era history, not a second dedicated citation for this specific tree. A Wikimedia Commons photo of the tree ('The Embankment Plane (6).jpg') was taken 19 September 2022, giving reasonably recent alive-evidence (about 4 years old). One historical superlative claim circulates ('one of the tallest London planes in the UK') that this pass could not independently verify against other city pages' claims; per hard rule 8 the writer should soften this to something like 'one of the tallest planes on the Embankment' or drop it rather than publish an unchecked superlative. Good material for the writer: this tree is a survivor of the very first scheme that made planting planes down a London thoroughfare fashionable, predating most of the city's plane-lined streets, standing where the Embankment meets the road up to Horse Guards and Whitehall.
